Description:Field of the invention

[0001] The present invention relates to material removal processes. More specifically, the present invention relates to a method for improving a material removal process.

Background of the invention:

[0002] In industries where precise control of light emission is essential, such as in backlit displays, architectural lighting, and automotive illumination systems, ensuring uniform light intensity across a surface presents a considerable challenge. Ensuring consistency of light intensity in series production of such products is also a considerable challenge. Light-emitting surfaces are typically created by etching or engraving materials, which allows light to pass through specific patterns or designs. Achieving the desired uniformity in light distribution is complex due to various external factors and inherent limitations in the engraving or etching process.
[0003] One of the significant issues in existing systems is their inability to adapt to environmental conditions that can affect the engraving or etching process. Factors such as ambient temperature and pressure of the surroundings can cause material distortions, affecting how the material reacts to the laser and, consequently, how the light passes through the engraved or etched surface. Fluctuations in temperature or pressure may lead to inconsistencies in material removal or cause the material to expand or contract slightly, altering the final light emission characteristics.
[0004] Often light emitting products are multilayer. For example, a light emitting surface has an additional spacer or diffuser layer on top of it to evenly distribute the light over the entire surface area or reduce the intensity of the light. The tolerances of the spacer/diffuser material thickness applied to the light-emitting surface can complicate achieving uniform light distribution. The variations in the spacer material thickness can impact how much light passes through the surface after etching or engraving. In some cases, the spacer material acts as a diffuser layer, and even minor deviations from the thickness can result in uneven light intensity. Current methods lack real-time adaptability to adjust for such variations in thickness during the process, leading to bright spots, dim areas, or irregular illumination.
[0005] Moreover, process tolerance in the engraving or etching is another major factor. Even with advanced machinery, deviations in the laser's precision, beam focus, or power can introduce small errors in the pattern being etched, affecting the light distribution. These tolerances in the process, especially when combined with variations in material properties, can lead to inconsistent removal of material, further leading to non-uniform light emission.
[0006] Current systems are typically designed with fixed operational parameters such as laser power, speed, and focal length, which are predefined and remain constant throughout the process. However, these parameters are not dynamically adjusted to account for real-time changes in environmental conditions or material tolerances. As a result, the final product often exhibits suboptimal light distribution, requiring additional adjustments, reworking, or even rejection of faulty products. This not only increases production costs but also reduces overall efficiency.
[0007] Therefore, there is a requirement for a method for improving the material removal processes to overcome all or a few drawbacks of the present technologies.

Objects of the invention

[0008] An object of the present invention is to provide a method for improving the material removal process. 
[0009] Another object of the present invention is to provide a method for improving a material removal process, which ensures consistent and even light distribution across the surface of an etched or engraved workpiece, reducing bright spots, dim areas, and inconsistencies in illumination. 
[0010] Yet another object of the present invention is to provide a method for improving a material removal process, which automatically adjusts the laser parameters during the material removal process to compensate for variations in material properties, environmental conditions, and process tolerances.
[0011] One more object of the present invention is to provide a method for improving a material removal process, which reduces the need for post-process corrections, reworking, or rejection of products due to non-uniform light distribution.

[0064] Further, the light source (20) is arranged on the material removal apparatus (10), around the workpiece (34). The light source (20) is specifically arranged at a predetermined location, the predetermined location is a place where the light source (20) is being arranged in the final product. [0065] Furthermore, the sensing unit (30) is arranged above the workpiece (34) to capture the images of the surface of the workpiece (34). Specifically, the sensing unit (30) is configured to capture an image of the surface of the workpiece (34) after each phase of material removal. The sensing unit (30) is a sensor adapted to capture the images of the workpiece (34) and communicate them with the processing unit (40). It may be obvious for a person skilled in the art to use any type of sensor/ unit to capture the image of the surface of the workpiece (34).
[0066] The images are captured to measure and detect lighting characteristics including color appearance such as color temperature, or color rendering index (CRI), luminous flux, illuminance, light beam angle, glare, dimming capability, uniformity, specifically, the light intensity and the light distribution emitted through the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34). The processing unit (40) is configured to compare the captured image (with or without additional image processing) with the reference image. The reference image is an image of the workpiece (34) of the final product, stored in the storage unit (60). The lighting characteristics of the captured image (with or without additional image processing) have to match the lighting characteristics of the reference image.
[0067] Specifically, the processing unit (40) is configured to adjust the light intensity and the light distribution of the captured image based on the properties of the diffuser layer (35) stored in the storage unit (60). The processing unit (40) is configured to calculate a light intensity reduction factor and a light intensity distribution factor based on the properties of the diffuser layer (35) stored in the storage unit (60) and apply the light intensity reduction factor and/or the light intensity distribution factor to the captured image to simulate the light intensity of the final product. The processing unit (40) is adapted to generate a processed image based on the properties of the diffuser layer (35) (as shown in figure 3b). The spacer layer or the diffuser layer (35) is placed above the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34) to evenly distribute or diffuse the light emitted through the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34).  
[0068] The diffuser layer (35) has physical properties such as thickness, transparency, refractive index, and light absorption characteristics. The physical properties are responsible for how light passes through the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34). For example, the thickness of the spacer can reduce or diffuse the light intensity emitted through the surface, while transparency or opacity is responsible for how much light can penetrate or reflect.
[0069] The storage unit (60) is being used to store the properties of the diffuser layer (35) before the first phase of material removal begins. The pre-stored properties of the diffuser layer (35) provide information about how light interacts with the diffuser layer (35) in the final product such as light intensity, light direction and light orientation. 
[0070] In an alternative embodiment, one or more of the processing unit (40), the storage unit (60), and the control unit (50) are remotely arranged away from the material removal apparatus (10) and adapted to communicate with the sensing unit (30) and the material removing head (15) through a wireless network.
[0071] Once, the sensing unit (30) captures the image of the material-removed surface, the processing unit (40) uses the properties of the diffuser layer (35) to adjust the light intensity and the light distribution of the captured image to generate the processed image simulating a light intensity of the workpiece (34) after application of the diffuser layer (35).
[0072] Further, the processing unit (40) is adapted to apply a virtual surface layer (36) (shown in figure 2) on the processed image to generate a secondary image simulating a real-life lighting characteristic of the final product. The virtual surface layer (36) imitates the characteristics of the actual surface layer of the final product which includes patterns, perforations, or other features. The virtual surface layer (36) is used to predict how light will behave once the actual surface layer is arranged over the diffuser layer which is arranged over the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34). The virtual surface layer (36) may have a predefined layout or pattern carved through the thickness of the layer allowing the light to transmit from a bottom surface to an upper surface. 
[0073] Specifically, the virtual surface layer (36) includes a plurality of perforations (not visible in figure 2) (shown in figure 3c) to form the predefined layout. The plurality of perforations is arranged adjacent to each other in a shape of the predefined layout. In the present embodiment, the perforations have a circular shape. In another embodiment, the perforations can be square, triangular or any other shape. The plurality of perforations shown in figure 3c   may also have perforations small enough to be unnoticeable and only the predefined layout is visible. The plurality of perforations is transparent on the virtual surface layer (36) so that light emitted from the workpiece (34) after the material removal process and diffuser layer (35) simulates the actual surface layer of the final product.
[0074] Moreover, the processing unit (40) compares the secondary image with the reference image to identify deviations in the lighting characteristics. The reference image is an image of the final product captured after laminating the diffuser layer (35) over the workpiece (34), an actual surface layer over the diffuser layer (35) and arranging the light source (200) arranged at the predefined location, thereby representing the real-life appearance of the product. In another aspect, the final product may consist of a single light emitting layer or two layers or four layers or any other number of layers. The processing (40) unit is adapted to superimpose a plurality of layers including plurality of diffuser layers or plurality of virtual surface layers based on the number of layers required in the final product.
[0075] The processing unit (40) compares the secondary image derived from the current state of the material-removed surface with the reference image indicative of the ideal image to identify any deviations or differences in the lighting characteristics between the secondary image and the reference image. 
[0076] In the present aspect of the invention, the reference image and the secondary image are divided into a grid having a plurality of cells. Each cell of the reference image has a corresponding cell of the secondary image. The corresponding cells of the reference image and the secondary image are with respect to the surface of the workpiece (34).  The first phase of the material removal is performed on a first cell of the grid using the predefined operational parameters. 
[0077] Furthermore, the processing unit (40) is adapted to modify the predefined operational parameters based on the identified deviations to generate the adjusted operational parameters. The processing unit (40) is adapted to define the adjusted operational parameters different from the predefined operational parameters based on the comparison between the secondary image and the reference image. The generated adjusted operational parameters are communicated with the control unit (50) to control the material removing head (15). 
[0078] Moreover, the processing unit (40) is adapted to control and modify the material removal patterns along with the predefined operational parameters. The material removalpatterns are specific configurations that determine how the material removal apparatus (10) interacts with the workpiece (34) during the material removal process specifically, how the material removing head (15) moves over the workpiece (34) to remove material according to the predefined layout (as shown in figure 3a). The material removal patterns define the method/steps used by the material removing head (15) to remove material from the surface, including the path, speed, and density of the lines. For example, the material removalpatterns may include line patterns, cross-hatching, dot matrix configurations, or other structured paths that control how the material removing head (15) moves across the workpiece (34) to create the predefined layout. 
[0079] If the material removal pattern is a line pattern, then by controlling the density of laser lines (measured in DPI or LPI) and the sequence of laser passes, the predefined layout is engraved with correct precision, depth, and light-diffusing properties. The material removal patterns are stored in the storage unit (60) and retrieved to perform the first phase of material removal on the workpiece (34). 
[0080] By way of a non-limiting example, the identified deviation and the adjusted operational parameters with modified material removal patterns are explained. If the light intensity of the material-removed surface is less than the light intensity of the reference image, one of the causes of this deviation might be the resolution, which is lines per inch. The lines per inch of the material removal pattern/design are responsible for the light intensity of the material-removed surface, if adjacent lines are away from each other, the light intensity emitting from the material-removed surface is less compared to the lines being closer to each other. When the material removing head (15) etches or engraves more lines in the first cell, the surface of the workpiece (34) will have finer details with less material remaining between the adjacent lines. The less distance between two adjacent lines allows more light to pass through, which increases the light intensity emitted through the material-removed surface. However, when fewer lines are etched or engraved, more material is left between the adjacent lines, which blocks the light or scatters the light unevenly. The blocking and/or scattering of the light may reduce the light intensity or cause uneven light distribution in the final product.
[0081] In another example, the processing unit (40) is adapted to modify the material removal patterns according to the shape of the predefined layout and the captured image. Referring to figures 4a-4c, the material removing head (15) is adapted to engrave the workpiece (34) according to the predefined layout shown in FIG. 4a. The predefined pattern includes two circular shapes (C1, C2) and the material removal pattern is a line pattern as shown in FIG. 4b. The line pattern has a length (L) and height (H) stored in the storage unit (60). 
[0082] The material removing head (15) starts the stroke from a starting point (S1) according to the predefined operational parameters such as the length and height (resolution in LPI) of the laser pattern as shown in figure 4b. Simultaneously, the sensing unit (30) captures the image and the processing unit (40) processes the image to detect the deviations. The processing unit (40) detects while material removal from the starting point (S1) to a finish point (S2), the shape of the predefined layout is gradually increasing and the light intensity detected by the captured image is not sufficient as compared to the intended light intensity in the final product. Accordingly, the processing unit (40) adjusts the predefined operational parameters and generates the adjusted operational parameters with adjusted pattern / design such as reduced height, thereby removing more material to allow more light to pass through the workpiece (34). 
[0083] As shown in figure 4c, at a central portion of the circular shape (C1), the material removal pattern is modified to have reduced height (H’), causing more material removal for higher-intensity light. Further, the reduced height (H’) is modified according to the gradually decreasing shape after the central portion towards the finish point (S2). Specifically, the reduced height (H’) is modified to the original height (H).
[0084] Furthermore, the processing unit (40) is adapted to adjust the height (H) of the line pattern for the subsequent circular shapes of the predefined layout (Figure 4c) based on the captured images. 
[0085] It may be obvious for a person skilled in the art to adjust the predefined operational parameters such as resolution in DPI or LPI according to the material removal pattern. If the material removal patterns are circles, then the density of the circles is modified to provide the intended results in the final product.
[0086] If the processing unit (40) detects that the light intensity of the secondary image is higher than that of the reference image, the processing unit (40) adjusts the resolution (lines per inch) by increasing the value of Lines Per Inch (LPI). The processing unit (40) modifies the predefined operational parameter which is resolution (LPI) and generates the adjusted operational parameter to communicate with the control unit (50).
[0087] The control unit (50) is connected to the processing unit (40) to receive the adjusted operational parameters and adjusted pattern / design. After receiving the adjusted operational parameters and adjusted pattern / design, the control unit (50) controls the material removing head (15) for a second phase of material removal. [00111] Referring now to figure 16, a method (200) for improving the material removal process in accordance with the present invention is illustrated. The method (200) is described in conjunction with the system (100) described above. The method (200) comprises steps of:
[00112] The method (200) starts at step (210).
[00113] At step (220), the material removing head (15) is adapted to perform a first phase of material removal on a portion of the surface of the workpiece (34). Before starting the first phase of material removal, the light source (20) is arranged around the workpiece (34)/connected to the workpiece (34) (in case the workpiece is the fabric which itself emits light) at the predefined position and is turned ON to simulate the real-life light emission through the material-removed surface. In the first phase, the control unit (50) controls the material removing head (15) according to predefined operational parameters. Further, the material removing head (15) is adapted to move over the surface of the workpiece (34) to remove the material (etch, engrave or the like) according to the predefined layout or pattern.
[00114] At step (230), the sensing unit (30) is adapted to capture the image of the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34). The captured image is then communicated with the processing unit (40) to generate the secondary image simulating real-life lighting characteristics and appearance of the final product. 
[00115] Specifically, in the first stage, the light intensity of the captured image is adjusted by the processing unit (40). The properties of the spacer layer (35) are stored in the storage unit (60) before initiating the material removal on the workpiece (34) which can be retrieved by the processing unit (40).  
[00116] Further, the processing unit (40) superimposes a virtual surface layer (36) over the processed image to generate the secondary image. [00117] At step (240), the secondary image generated in step (230) is compared with the reference image of the final product. The reference image is previously stored in the storage unit (60) and is retrieved by the processing unit (40) to compare it with the secondary image. Specifically, the processing unit (40) compares the lighting characteristics such as light intensity and the light distribution of the secondary image against the reference image to identify deviations in the lighting characteristics including light intensity and the light distribution/light uniformity. 
[00118] At step (250), the identified deviations are used to define the adjusted operational parameters. The processing unit (40) is adapted to define the adjusted operational parameters and material removal (such as etching, engraving or the like) design or pattern different from the predefined operational parameters and material removal (etching, engraving or the like) design or pattern based on the comparison between the secondary image and the reference image. The adjusted operational parameters and adjusted material removal pattern are communicated with the control unit (50) to control the material removing head (15) to perform a second phase of material removal over a corresponding portion of the surface according to the adjusted operational parameters and adjusted material removal pattern to achieve desired lighting characteristics such as uniform light intensity and distribution. 
[00119] At step (260), the processing unit (40) repeats steps (230) to (250) until each phase of the material removal has been performed on the workpiece (34). The processing unit (40) detects whether all the phases have been performed or not and if all the phases have not been done, the processing unit (40) sends a signal to the sensing unit (30) to capture the image of the workpiece (34) for comparing it with the reference image. If the processing unit (40) detects that all the phases of the material removal have been done, the method (200) ends at step (270).
[00120] In an additional embodiment, the method (200) for improving material removal is configured to convert the captured images into a greyscale image before generating the processed image.
[00121] Specifically, after the sensing unit (30) captures an image of the light distribution through the material-removed surface of the workpiece (34), the processing unit (40) converts the captured image into a greyscale image. The processing unit (40) uses the greyscale image to generate a processed image that simulates the light distribution through the material-removed surface.
[00122] After generating the processed image, the processing unit (40) superimposes a virtual surface layer (36) to produce a secondary image, which simulates the real-life light behavior of the final product or intended workpiece (34). The secondary image is also in greyscale and is compared with a reference image stored in the storage unit (60). The reference image is stored as a greyscale image for comparison with the secondary image.
[00123] The comparison between the secondary image (greyscale) and the reference image (greyscale) allows the processing unit (40) to detect deviations in the lighting characteristics including light intensity or distribution. Based on the detected deviations, the processing unit (40) adjusts the predefined operational parameters, such as laser power or resolution (LPI), to create adjusted operational parameters and the adjusted material removal pattern or layout that controls the material removing head (15) during subsequent phases of material removal. BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACE SYSTEM UTILIZING VISUALLY EVOKED POTENTIALS FOR COMMUNICATION AND COGNITIVE REHABILITATION AND METHOD THEREOF Disclosed is a gaze communication system (100) that includes a sensing unit (102) and a processor (104). The sensing unit (102) is configured to sense a plurality of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals associated with a user. The processor (104) is coupled to the sensing unit (102), and configured to filter the EEG signals to remove noise and artifacts from EEG data associated with the EEG signals. The processor (104) is configured to extract a plurality of features associated with Visually Evoked Potentials (VEP) of the user. The processor (104) is configured to identify VEP corresponding to at least one visual stimulus associated with the user. The VEP corresponding to the at least one visual stimulus is identified by way of classification of the plurality of features. FIG. 1is the reference figure.

Feature Components for VEP Identification:

The system’s feature extraction process identifies distinct VEP components such as P100, N75, and N145. These components are well-documented in neuroscience as critical markers of visual processing in the brain.
P100 Component: Known for its robust and consistent response, this component represents early visual processing.
N75 Component: This component reflects initial neural activity upon exposure to visual stimuli.
N145 Component: Occurring later in the visual processing chain, this component provides additional granularity to the user’s neural response.

Machine Learning for VEP Classification:
The classification of VEPs is facilitated by advanced machine learning techniques. These algorithms analyze patterns within the extracted features to accurately map them to corresponding visual stimuli.

Machine learning models are trained using extensive datasets, ensuring they adapt to individual user variations and environmental conditions. This adaptability enhances the system's robustness and accuracy, making it reliable across diverse use cases.

Prediction for Enhanced User Interaction:
The processor (104) generates prediction signals that enhance the system’s communication efficiency. For instance, based on the user’s previous selections or gaze patterns, the system suggests likely visual information.

This predictive feature minimizes effort and reduces cognitive load for the user, particularly beneficial for individuals with severe impairments. It enables faster communication by streamlining the selection process.

Selection Mechanism and Feedback Generation:
The gaze-controlled communication device includes a selection mechanism that is triggered upon identifying VEPs corresponding to specific visual stimuli.

Recommendation-Based Interaction: The system provides recommendations to the user, such as specific letters, words, or phrases, based on their gaze focus. Upon selection, the system generates a feedback signal to confirm the user’s choice.

This mechanism ensures accuracy and reinforces user actions, creating a fluid interaction loop that is critical for effective communication.

Visual Feedback: Highlighting selected options on the screen to confirm user actions.

Haptic Feedback: Delivering vibrations through wearable devices to provide tactile confirmation.

Auditory Feedback: Playing audio prompts or confirmations for accessibility, especially for users with visual impairments.

This multimodal feedback mechanism ensures the system caters to a wide range of user preferences and needs, making it universally accessible and effective.

The gaze communication system described in the claims can be implemented using advanced sensing, signal processing, machine learning, and feedback technologies.

Sensing Unit and EEG Signal Acquisition: The system employs an EEG sensing unit capable of capturing brain activity with high precision. Devices such as the EmotivEpoc+ or OpenBCI EEG Systems are ideal for this purpose. These devices use non-invasive electrodes to record EEG signals from the user's scalp. Signal acquisition software processes these recordings in real time to ensure the data is suitable for downstream analysis. To ensure signal quality, these systems can implement real-time impedance checks and adaptive noise suppression techniques, reducing interference from muscle movements or environmental noise.

Signal Pre-Processing and Feature Extraction: Once the EEG signals are captured, they are filtered and pre-processed to remove noise and artifacts. Techniques such as band-pass filtering (e.g., 1-50 Hz) and Independent Component Analysis (ICA) are employed to isolate the neural signals corresponding to visual stimuli. This step ensures that only the most relevant EEG data is analyzed further.

The processed signals are then passed through a feature extraction algorithm. The system specifically identifies the P100, N75, and N145 components, which are distinct markers of visually evoked potentials (VEPs). Time-domain analysis can be used to locate these components, while wavelet transforms or Fourier transforms may extract additional frequency-domain features. These extracted features are crucial for distinguishing the user's response to visual stimuli.

Classification of Visually Evoked Potentials: Machine learning techniques play a pivotal role in classifying the extracted VEP features. Algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, or Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are trained on labeled datasets containing EEG recordings corresponding to known visual stimuli. For instance, if the system uses CNNs, it processes the extracted features as input vectors, allowing the model to identify the VEP patterns with high accuracy.

Real-time classification is achieved using lightweight implementations of these algorithms, optimized for execution on edge devices or processors integrated within the system. By associating specific VEP patterns with the visual stimuli displayed on the user interface, the system can reliably interpret the user’s intent.

Gaze-Controlled Communication Interface and User Interaction: The system features an intuitive gaze-controlled interface. This interface, displayed on a tablet or monitor, presents letters, words, or phrases as selectable options. Visual stimuli are dynamically updated based on user progress and preferences. Algorithms like saliency mapping can enhance visual elements, ensuring they effectively capture the user’s gaze.

When a user focuses on a specific visual stimulus, the system detects and classifies the associated VEP. A selection mechanism is triggered, and the system provides a recommendation, such as predicting the user’s next word or phrase based on their previous selections. Predictive text algorithms, similar to those used in smartphones, are integrated into this process, significantly improving the speed of communication.

Feedback Mechanism and Multimodal Reinforcement: The system’s feedback unit delivers real-time responses to the user. For instance, when the system detects and confirms a selection, it visually highlights the chosen letter or phrase on the screen. Simultaneously, auditory feedback, such as a confirmation beep, is played to reinforce the action. For users requiring additional confirmation, haptic feedback is delivered through wearable devices like smartwatches or vibration modules.

The feedback loop employs algorithms to adaptively adjust the feedback intensity based on user preferences and performance. For example, reinforcement learning algorithms can fine-tune the feedback over time, ensuring it remains engaging and non-intrusive.

Performance Monitoring and Analytics:
To track user progress and system effectiveness, the system includes a robust data logging and analytics module. EEG data, VEP classification results, and user interactions are recorded during each session. Analytics tools use time-series analysis and statistical models to identify trends in user performance, such as improved accuracy in gaze selections or reduced response times.

These insights are visualized on a therapist dashboard, enabling healthcare providers to customize therapy sessions based on the user’s needs. The system can also employ predictive analytics to forecast user performance, assisting therapists in planning long-term rehabilitation strategies.

Integration of Advanced Prediction and Selection Mechanisms: The processor generates prediction signals to assist users in their interactions. For instance, if a user frequently selects certain words, the system prioritizes those options using algorithms such as Markov chains or recurrent neural networks (RNNs). These algorithms learn from user patterns, providing personalized suggestions that minimize cognitive load.

Upon detecting a VEP corresponding to a particular visual stimulus, the gaze-controlled device triggers a selection mechanism. This mechanism relies on real-time decision trees to confirm the user's intent and execute the corresponding action. Feedback is generated based on this action, closing the interaction loop effectively.

System Scalability and Adaptability: The system is designed to be hardware-agnostic, supporting a wide range of EEG devices and display technologies. For example, it can integrate with virtual reality (VR) headsets for immersive therapy sessions or standard monitors for conventional rehabilitation setups. Its modular software architecture supports API integrations, allowing compatibility with telehealth platforms or other assistive technologies.

In conclusion, the implementation of this gaze communication system leverages cutting-edge techniques in sensing, signal processing, machine learning, and feedback delivery to provide a robust, adaptive, and user-friendly solution. This real-world approach ensures the system meets diverse user needs, making it a versatile tool for communication and cognitive rehabilitation.

To summarize, the method (200) outlines a systematic approach for using visually evoked potentials (VEPs) to facilitate communication and cognitive rehabilitation. The process begins with sensing (202) electroencephalogram (EEG) signals using advanced EEG sensors such as EmotivEpoc+, OpenBCI EEG Systems, or Muse devices. These non-invasive sensors capture neural activity generated in response to visual stimuli presented to the user. Integrated multi-bio-signal systems like Empatica E4 or Shimmer3 can also enhance signal acquisition by combining EEG data with additional physiological parameters for improved accuracy.

After acquiring the EEG signals, the processor (104) initiates filtering and pre-processing (204). This step involves removing noise and artifacts from the raw EEG data using advanced signal processing techniques, such as band-pass filtering or Independent Component Analysis (ICA). The clean data is then subjected to feature extraction (206), focusing on identifying key VEP components like P100, N75, and N145. These components are essential markers of the user’s neural response to visual stimuli and are extracted using time-domain and frequency-domain analysis.

The extracted features are subsequently classified and identified (208) by the processor using machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM) or Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This classification associates specific VEPs with visual stimuli displayed on the user interface (106). Once VEPs are identified, the gaze-controlled communication device (110) provides real-time feedback (210) to the user. This feedback includes recommendations for selecting letters, words, or phrases displayed on the user interface. The selection mechanism is triggered upon detecting the relevant VEPs, and the system generates a feedback signal confirming the user’s choice, enabling seamless interaction.

The method further provides additional functionalities to enhance the user’s interaction with the system. The user interface (106) displays visual information, such as letters, words, or phrases, prompting the user to generate a visual stimulus in response. For example, focusing on a specific letter triggers the sensing of VEPs, which are processed to identify the user’s intent. The interface design ensures clarity and accessibility, facilitating effortless gaze communication.

To improve efficiency, the method includes generating a prediction signal based on user behaviour. For instance, if a user frequently selects specific words, predictive algorithms such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suggest probable next words or phrases. This predictive capability reduces cognitive effort and accelerates communication, making the system highly adaptive to individual user patterns.

Upon generating a feedback signal, the system provides multimodal feedback to confirm user actions. This feedback can be visual (highlighting the selected option), haptic (vibrations through a wearable device), or auditory (spoken confirmation). These feedback mechanisms not only enhance user confidence but also make the system inclusive for individuals with varying sensory abilities. The integration of these features ensures a robust, intuitive, and efficient interaction process, advancing both communication and cognitive rehabilitation.

From implementation perspective, following techniques can be used to implement the invention:

Sensing EEG Signals (202): To sense EEG signals associated with visually evoked potentials (VEPs), advanced non-invasive devices like EmotivEpoc+, OpenBCI EEG Systems, Muse 2, or Muse S can be utilized. These devices use dry or semi-dry electrodes for high-quality signal acquisition, reducing the need for extensive preparation while maintaining reliable contact with the scalp. For more comprehensive analysis, integrated multi-bio-signal systems like Empatica E4 or Shimmer3 can complement EEG data with physiological measurements such as heart rate variability or skin conductance, providing additional insights into the user's state during the session.These systems are often paired with proprietary software development kits (SDKs) or APIs that allow real-time data acquisition and synchronization. Techniques like real-time impedance monitoring ensure the electrodes maintain optimal contact, while dynamic sampling rate adjustments (e.g., 128 Hz to 256 Hz) enable high-resolution capture of neural signals for precise VEP detection.

Filtering and Pre-Processing (204): The EEG signals acquired are pre-processed to remove noise and artifacts caused by muscle movements, electrical interference, or other external factors. Signal processing modules use techniques such as band-pass filtering to isolate frequencies within the 1–50 Hz range, where VEP components typically occur. Adaptive noise cancellation methods can be applied to further enhance signal quality, dynamically suppressing interference without distorting relevant neural activity.Independent Component Analysis (ICA) or Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is used to separate and identify noise sources, such as eye blinks or muscle artifacts, which are then excluded from the dataset. Additionally, techniques like wavelet denoising are employed to preserve the temporal characteristics of the VEP signals while eliminating high-frequency noise.

Feature Extraction (206): Feature extraction focuses on identifying critical components of VEPs, such as P100, N75, and N145, which are indicative of the user's neural response to visual stimuli. These components are extracted using time-domain analysis, where peak latencies and amplitudes are measured directly from the EEG signal. Frequency-domain techniques, such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) or wavelet transform, are used to analyze oscillatory patterns associated with VEPs. These techniques provide insights into how neural responses evolve over time, crucial for distinguishing between different types of stimuli. In some cases, advanced approaches like Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) are utilized to decompose complex signals into intrinsic mode functions, isolating features that may not be apparent using traditional methods.

Classification and Identification of VEPs (208): Machine learning algorithms play a vital role in classifying and identifying VEPs. Supervised learning techniques, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM) or Random Forests, are commonly employed to map the extracted features to specific visual stimuli. These models are trained on datasets containing labeled EEG recordings, allowing them to learn patterns associated with different VEP responses.For more dynamic and adaptable systems, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are used. CNNs process the extracted EEG features as input vectors, enabling high-accuracy classification by identifying intricate patterns in the data. Additionally, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly those utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units, are employed to account for the temporal dependencies in EEG signals, ensuring reliable classification even under varying conditions.

Providing Real-Time Feedback (210): Once VEPs are identified, the system provides real-time feedback to the user through a gaze-controlled communication device. The processor generates recommendations based on the detected VEPs, such as selecting specific letters, words, or phrases displayed on a user interface. Predictive algorithms like Markov Chains or recurrent neural networks (RNNs) enhance this process by anticipating the user's next selection based on their interaction history, improving the speed and efficiency of communication.The feedback loop employs multimodal responses to confirm the user’s actions. For instance, visual feedback highlights the selected option on the screen, while auditory feedback provides a confirmation tone. Tactile feedback, such as gentle vibrations, can also be delivered via wearable devices, ensuring inclusivity for users with varying sensory preferences. Real-time feedback ensures a seamless user experience, allowing for continuous and intuitive interaction.

This integration of advanced techniques and algorithms enables a robust, adaptive, and user-friendly implementation of the described method for utilizing VEPs in communication and cognitive rehabilitation.

COGNITIVE REHABILITATION SYSTEM THAT UTILIZES INTERACTION BETWEENMUSIC AND BRAIN ACTIVITY AND METHOD THEREOF The cognitive rehabilitation system (100) is designed to support emotional and cognitive well-being through personalized music therapy. It includes a sensing unit (102) that detects a variety of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals from the user, capturing key brainwave activity. A processor (104) works in tandem with the sensing unit to process these signals by filtering out noise and artifacts, refining the data for accurate analysis. The processor then extracts several features linked to the user’s emotional and cognitive state, such as alpha, beta, and gamma rhythms. Based on these extracted features, the system identifies the user’s emotional state and selects appropriate music to address it. The system then delivers the music as part of a tailored neurofeedback exercises aimed at promoting cognitive rehabilitation. This approach not only targets emotional regulation but also enhances cognitive function through music-driven therapeutic interventions. FIG. 1is the reference figure.

TECHNICAL FIELD

The present disclosure relates generally to the field of Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications, particularly those involving music therapy and neurofeedback for cognitive and emotional rehabilitation. More specifically, it pertains to a system and method for utilizing electroencephalogram (EEG) data to dynamically customize and deliver music neurofeedback exercises tailored to a user’s cognitive and emotional states.

BACKGROUND

Music therapy is widely acknowledged as a powerful approach for enhancing emotional regulation and cognitive functioning. However, traditional methods are often static, failing to account for the dynamic nature of a user's real-time mental and emotional states. This lack of adaptability can result in less effective therapeutic outcomes, particularly for individuals requiring tailored interventions. Moreover, these traditional approaches do not provide quantitative feedback, leaving therapists and users with limited insights into the therapy's effectiveness or the user’s progress.

Recent advancements in Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) technology, especially those leveraging EEG-based systems, offer promising solutions by enabling direct monitoring of neural activity. These systems open the door to creating personalized therapeutic experiences that can dynamically respond to a user’s mental state. However, many existing BCI applications are limited in scope, focusing either on data acquisition or basic neurofeedback, without incorporating features like real-time signal processing or adaptive content delivery. This fragmented approach reduces the overall potential of BCI-driven therapies.

Despite significant progress, there is a clear need for a comprehensive system that integrates EEG monitoring, advanced signal processing, and real-time customization of therapeutic content, such as music. Current solutions often lack accessibility, are not user-friendly, or fail to provide engaging and sustained interactions, further limiting their impact. Addressing these challenges requires a robust, adaptive platform capable of delivering meaningful, effective, and engaging therapeutic interventions tailored to the unique neural patterns and emotional needs of each user. 

Thus, there is a need for a technical solution that overcomes the aforementioned problems of conventional techniques.

SUMMARY

Disclosed is a cognitive rehabilitation system. The system includes a sensing unit and a processor. The sensing unit is configured to sense a plurality of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals associated with a user. The processor is coupled to the sensing unit. The processor is configured to filter the EEG signals to remove noise and artifacts from EEG data associated with the EEG signals. The processor is further configured to extract a plurality of features associated with emotional and cognitive state. The plurality of features comprising alpha rhythms, beta rhythms, and gamma rhythms. The processor is further configured to identify an emotional state of the user based on the plurality of features. The processor is further configured to facilitate music selection and delivery based on the emotional state of the user. The processor is further configured to generate a neurofeedback exercises based on the music selection and delivery. The neurofeedback exercises facilitate cognitive rehabilitation for the emotional state of the user. 

The present invention introduces a system and method for music-based cognitive and emotional rehabilitation utilizing a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI). This system is designed to leverage real-time EEG signal acquisition to create personalized therapeutic interventions. It includes a sensing unit to capture EEG signals, a processor to analyse these signals, and a feedback unit that delivers customized music therapy and neurofeedback exercises. By filtering EEG data and extracting features related to cognitive and emotional states, the processor adapts music therapy to align with the user’s unique neural activity.

Central to the system is a user interface that empowers therapists and users with intuitive tools for therapy customization and monitoring. The interface facilitates real-time interaction, enabling therapists to adjust therapeutic parameters dynamically while also offering users insights into their progress. This user-centric design ensures that neurofeedback exercises are both engaging and tailored to individual needs, optimizing the rehabilitation process.

To enhance therapeutic outcomes, the system incorporates advanced tracking and analytics features. It logs user performance data across sessions, generating comprehensive reports that therapists can use to refine treatment strategies. These analytics offer a deeper understanding of user progress, supporting data-driven adjustments that improve the efficacy of therapy. Additionally, the ability to visualize trends and metrics over time ensures that the system can address evolving user requirements effectively.

The system’s modular architecture ensures compatibility with a wide range of EEG devices and audio platforms, making it highly adaptable for diverse applications. Its flexible design allows deployment in clinical settings, at home, or in research environments, catering to a broad spectrum of users. By integrating real-time adaptability, user-friendly interfaces, and robust analytics, this invention provides a versatile and powerful solution for cognitive and emotional rehabilitation through music therapy.

To summarize, the present invention pertains to a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) application designed to leverage the interplay between music and brain activity for cognitive and emotional rehabilitation. The system integrates EEG-based monitoring with advanced signal processing and machine learning techniques to tailor music therapy and neurofeedback exercises, enhancing therapeutic outcomes by dynamically adapting to the user’s cognitive and emotional state.

The system begins by acquiring EEG signals through a non-invasive sensing unit during music therapy and neurofeedback sessions. The EEG headset captures neural activity across multiple brain regions, focusing on rhythms such as alpha, beta, and gamma waves that correlate with cognitive and emotional states. For instance, alpha rhythms may indicate relaxation, while beta rhythms can reflect focused attention.

To ensure accurate analysis, the processor filters the EEG signals to remove noise and artifacts using techniques like Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and bandpass filtering. These preprocessing steps are essential for isolating brain activity from external disturbances, such as muscle movements or environmental interference. The system then extracts features, identifying relevant rhythms and patterns linked to emotional states, such as stress or calmness, and cognitive functions like memory and attention.

The processor employs machine learning techniques, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), to classify the extracted features. For example, if the EEG signals reveal heightened beta activity, the system might identify a state of cognitive engagement and select music tracks that enhance focus or relaxation, depending on therapeutic goals.

A unique aspect of the invention is its ability to dynamically customize music therapy based on real-time EEG data. A music selection algorithm analyzes the user’s brain state and adjusts the tempo, rhythm, and melody of the music to achieve optimal therapeutic effects. For example, calming music might be delivered during stress episodes, while upbeat tunes could stimulate engagement during cognitive tasks. The music delivery system adapts continuously, ensuring a seamless and personalized therapeutic experience.

The system also includes interactive neurofeedback exercises that use music to enhance cognitive functions and emotional regulation. For instance, users might perform tasks where their progress triggers changes in the music, reinforcing desired brain states. Real-time feedback—delivered through auditory, visual, or haptic cues—guides the user during these exercises, promoting a stronger connection between cognitive efforts and therapeutic outcomes.

To monitor progress, the system logs EEG data, neurofeedback performance, and music selections for each session. An analytics dashboard allows therapists and users to track changes in emotional and cognitive states over time, providing insights through visualizations like trend graphs and heat maps. Detailed progress reports highlight metrics such as improvements in memory or reductions in stress, enabling therapists to refine therapy plans.

The invention also facilitates therapist interaction through an intuitive user interface. Therapists can select music types, adjust therapy parameters, and monitor real-time progress. For example, if a user’s EEG data shows insufficient relaxation during therapy, the therapist can modify the session by switching to a more calming music genre. The interface ensures transparency and adaptability, allowing therapists to optimize each session according to the user’s needs.

In conclusion, this BCI-based cognitive rehabilitation system combines advanced EEG monitoring, machine learning algorithms, and real-time music customization to deliver highly personalized therapy. By dynamically adapting to the user’s brain state, the system offers an innovative and effective approach to improving cognitive functions and emotional regulation, making it a valuable tool in modern therapeutic practices.

Further, the present invention provides, a method for facilitating cognitive rehabilitation by leveraging EEG signals and music therapy. The process begins with the sensing of EEG signals during music therapy and neurofeedback sessions. A non-invasive EEG headset is used to acquire these signals, capturing brain activity in real-time. These signals represent various neural oscillations, such as alpha rhythms (associated with relaxation), beta rhythms (linked to attention and cognitive engagement), and gamma rhythms (connected to higher-order cognitive functions). Advanced EEG acquisition systems ensure accurate and consistent data collection, even in dynamic environments.

After acquisition, the EEG signals are filtered to remove noise and artifacts. Common preprocessing techniques include bandpass filtering, which isolates relevant frequency bands (e.g., 8–13 Hz for alpha rhythms), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), which separates and eliminates artifacts caused by eye blinks or muscle movements. These steps are critical to ensure that the EEG data accurately reflects the user's cognitive and emotional states.

The filtered signals are then subjected to feature extraction to identify meaningful patterns. Techniques such as Fourier Transform or Wavelet Transform are applied to decompose EEG signals into their constituent rhythms. Machine learning algorithms like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) may also be employed to reduce dimensionality while preserving critical information about the user's brain states. These features help in understanding the user's current emotional and cognitive conditions.

The next step involves identifying the user’s emotional state based on the extracted features. This is achieved through advanced classification algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) or Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which are trained on labeled EEG datasets to recognize patterns associated with various emotional states (e.g., stress, calmness, or focus). For example, an increase in beta activity combined with suppressed alpha rhythms might indicate heightened stress or alertness.

Based on the identified emotional state, the system facilitates music selection and delivery. A music recommendation algorithm, incorporating techniques like Collaborative Filtering or Reinforcement Learning, dynamically selects and modifies music tracks. Parameters such as tempo, melody, and rhythm are adjusted to align with the user’s current state. For instance, soothing melodies may be chosen to alleviate stress, while rhythmic tracks might be used to improve focus during cognitive exercises.

The processor then generates neurofeedback exercises tailored to the user’s needs. These exercises involve interactive tasks where the user’s brain activity influences the therapy in real-time. For example, in a neurofeedback session, the user’s ability to maintain specific brainwave patterns (e.g., alpha dominance for relaxation) might dynamically control the progression of the music, reinforcing desired cognitive or emotional states.

To ensure a comprehensive approach, the method incorporates progress tracking by generating detailed reports. The progress report includes historical cognitive data, such as EEG responses, music selections, and task performance over time. These reports are visualized through analytics dashboards, enabling therapists to assess the effectiveness of therapy and make informed adjustments.

The method further provides feedback signals based on the progress report. For instance, if a user demonstrates improved relaxation patterns, the processor may generate a feedback signal that is communicated through visual cues (e.g., calming visuals on a screen), haptic feedback (e.g., a gentle vibration), or auditory signals (e.g., affirming tones). This multimodal feedback system enhances the user’s engagement and reinforces positive therapeutic outcomes.

Overall, the invention integrates sophisticated techniques and algorithms to create a personalized and adaptive cognitive rehabilitation system. By dynamically combining EEG analysis, music therapy, neurofeedback, and real-time feedback, the method delivers an effective and user-centric approach to improving emotional and cognitive well-being.

Real-World Implementation: Cognitive Rehabilitation System for Workplace Stress Management

A multinational corporation implements a cognitive rehabilitation system in its workplace wellness program to address employee stress and enhance productivity. The system integrates the described invention, leveraging EEG-based music therapy and neurofeedback for cognitive and emotional rehabilitation.

Setting and User Engagement
Employees are provided access to relaxation pods equipped with non-invasive EEG headsets, a processor unit, and an interactive display. These pods allow employees to engage in personalized therapy sessions during breaks or after work hours.

1. Sensing EEG Signals:
When an employee enters the pod, they wear the EEG headset, which begins monitoring brain activity. For example, an employee experiencing workplace stress might exhibit heightened beta rhythms and reduced alpha rhythms. These signals are continuously recorded during the session, capturing brain activity in real-time.

2. Filtering EEG Signals:
The processor pre-processes the EEG signals by applying bandpass filters to isolate frequencies relevant to stress detection (e.g., alpha and beta rhythms). Techniques like Independent Component Analysis (ICA) are used to remove artifacts from muscle movements or eye blinks, ensuring that the data reflects the employee's genuine cognitive and emotional state.

3. Extracting Features:
Using Fourier Transform and machine learning-based feature extraction techniques, the processor identifies specific patterns in the EEG data. For instance, suppressed alpha rhythms combined with elevated beta activity indicate stress or anxiety. Gamma rhythms may also be monitored to assess focus and problem-solving capabilities.

4. Identifying Emotional State:
Based on the extracted features, the processor uses a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model to classify the employee’s emotional state. In this example, the system determines the user is experiencing stress.

5. Facilitating Music Selection and Delivery:
The processor dynamically curates a playlist tailored to the user's emotional state. For stress, the system selects slow-tempo instrumental tracks with calming melodies. A music recommendation algorithm adapts the playlist in real-time as the employee's brain activity shifts toward a more relaxed state.

6. Generating Neurofeedback Exercises:
The system introduces an interactive neurofeedback game where the employee’s brain activity influences the progression of visuals on the display. For instance, maintaining a relaxed alpha-dominant brainwave state causes a serene landscape to brighten, reinforcing the user’s relaxation. These exercises train the user to regulate stress responses effectively.

7. Generating Personalized Cognitive Training:
After the session, the processor designs follow-up activities, such as interactive cognitive puzzles or memory games, which the employee can access via a mobile app. These exercises target specific cognitive functions (e.g., attention or memory), enhancing workplace performance over time.

8. Progress Report and Feedback:
At the end of each session, the system generates a detailed progress report. For example, it might highlight how the employee's stress levels decreased during the session, represented through a combination of alpha rhythm enhancement and beta rhythm reduction. This report is accessible via an analytics dashboard for both the employee and the wellness coach.

A feedback signal is also generated, providing real-time auditory cues (e.g., calming tones) and visual affirmations (e.g., a congratulatory message) to reinforce positive behaviour. Haptic feedback, such as a gentle vibration on a wristband, may be used to indicate milestones achieved during the session.

Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention in general relates to the management and biodegradation of solid waste. More particularly, the present invention relates to a biodigester for management and biodegradation of human waste in high altitude regions.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Ensuring proper sanitation is crucial for maintaining public health, as inadequate waste disposal is a major source of pathogenic contamination, affecting soil, water, and air. With the global increase in population and rapid urbanization, existing waste management infrastructure is under immense strain, demanding the development of more efficient, sustainable systems for human waste treatment. Anaerobic digestion, or methanization, is a biological process that decomposes organic material, including human waste, under anaerobic (oxygen-deprived) conditions. This process generates biogas, predominantly methane, which can be harnessed as a renewable energy source. Additionally, it produces biosolids (sludge) and grey water, which can be repurposed as fertilizers. Biodigesters are engineered systems designed to optimize this anaerobic digestion process. These systems can be deployed at varying scales, converting human waste into valuable resources such as biogas for energy and grey water for agricultural use.
Several biodigester technologies exist in the prior art, each addressing different aspects of waste treatment:
1595/DEL/2006 describes an anaerobic digester designed for public transportation systems. The digester uses a dual-stage process combining biological and chemical treatment to degrade human waste.
WO2012042526A1 describes a self-sustaining biodigester designed for onboard applications, which integrates anaerobic biodegradation with chemical treatment, ensuring safe disposal of human waste in various environments.
2375/DEL/2010 describes a modular, stainless-steel biodigester intended for use in public transport vehicles. The system is divided into six chambers, each separated by partitions, and features a biological treatment component, a chlorinator for chemical treatment, and a non-biodegradable waste elimination mechanism. The system facilitates microbial activity through immobilization matrices and disinfects waste prior to disposal.
US13876791A1 describes a public transportation sanitation system by employing anaerobic digestion to minimize environmental impact. The document describes that the system is particularly effective at preventing non-biodegradable materials from entering the system, enhancing the ecological sustainability of waste treatment processes.
US7560026B2 describes a two-stage anaerobic digester, combining mesophilic and thermophilic digestion stages. The system optimizes waste decomposition through precise temperature control, mild agitation, and heat recovery mechanisms. 
Although several systems are available and offer significant advancements, however they are predominantly designed for tropical climates, operating effectively in temperature ranges between 20°C and 50°C. Further, the available systems focus on biogas generation and fertilizer production under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions. However, they are ill-suited for high-altitude or extremely cold environments, where ambient temperatures can drop below -30°C, often reaching -40°C. In such conditions, conventional biodigesters face operational challenges, including freezing of components, pipe blockages, and severe limitations in microbial activity, making effective sanitation nearly impossible. Given these limitations, human waste disposal in remote, high-altitude, and low-temperature regions remains a pressing issue. The slow rate of natural biodegradation in such environments exacerbates the problem, leading to unsanitary conditions and heightened health risks.
To address these challenges, there is an urgent need for an advanced biodigester capable of functioning in extreme low-temperature environments. The present invention responds to this need by offering an eco-friendly, cost-effective, and portable solution that can operate in high-altitude, sub-zero regions with minimal water consumption. Designed to be lightweight, efficient, and resilient, this biodigester represents a breakthrough in sustainable sanitation technology, ensuring reliable waste treatment even in the harshest environmental conditions.

The biodigester employs a commercially available blend of microbial bacteria, specifically selected and acclimated for this application. The digestion process is carried out in four sequential stages:
Hydrolysis: In this initial phase, hydrolytic bacteria break down complex organic polymers into simpler monomers, such as sugars, which can then be processed by other bacteria.
Acidogenesis: This phase involves the conversion of these monomers into volatile fatty acids, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide by acidogenic bacteria.
Acetogenesis: During this stage, acetogenic bacteria convert the volatile fatty acids into acetic acid, along with additional hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
Methanogenesis: The final stage involves methanogenic bacteria converting acetic acid and hydrogen into methane and carbon dioxide, resulting in the production of biogas.
The biogas generated is primarily composed of methane and carbon dioxide, while the residual solid material (sludge) and liquid (grey water) remain mineral-rich. These byproducts can be repurposed as fertilizer following appropriate post-treatment processes.

The present invention pertains to wearable health technologies and personalized healthcare systems. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Elderly individuals are particularly vulnerable to temperature fluctuations due to age-related physiological changes. Existing solutions, such as generic wearable devices or household climate control systems, lack personalization and adaptability to individual thermal comfort needs. Furthermore, these systems fail to monitor real-time body temperature and environmental conditions simultaneously, resulting in suboptimal solutions for maintaining elderly comfort and health.
Current wearable devices focus primarily on fitness tracking or basic health monitoring. They do not offer integrated functionalities for regulating body temperature based on personalized requirements. Similarly, existing household climate control systems operate at a macro level, failing to address localized needs for specific individuals, particularly the elderly. The absence of adaptive, real-time solutions limits the effectiveness of these technologies in addressing thermal comfort challenges.
This invention addresses these limitations by introducing a wearable device equipped with IoT and AI capabilities. The system monitors real-time body temperature, external environmental factors, and activity levels, dynamically adjusting thermal outputs to maintain an optimal comfort zone. By integrating advanced sensor technologies, machine learning algorithms, and user-specific data, the invention offers a comprehensive solution for elderly thermal regulation.

The IoT-Driven Artificial Intelligence-Based Personalized Wearable Body Temperature Controlling Device for Elderly is a smart, adaptive system designed to ensure thermal comfort and safety during household activities. The device integrates wearable sensors, an intelligent processing unit, and a temperature control mechanism, all interconnected through IoT for seamless operation.
The system continuously monitors body temperature, external environmental conditions, and user activity levels using a combination of biological and environmental sensors. Data collected is processed through AI algorithms, which analyze patterns and predict optimal thermal outputs for maintaining comfort. The device dynamically adjusts its thermal mechanisms, such as heating or cooling pads, based on real-time data and individual preferences.
The invention features an intuitive user interface for customization and monitoring. Users or caregivers can access and control device settings through a mobile application or wearable interface. Conventional mixing blades used in kitchen appliances often struggle to achieve uniform consistency, particularly with dense batters. These inefficiencies lead to longer mixing times, uneven textures, and suboptimal results in baking or cooking.
Existing batter mixing attachments often feature generic designs that are not optimized for thorough blending. These limitations are particularly pronounced when dealing with thick or high-viscosity mixtures.
This invention addresses these shortcomings by introducing a batter blade attachment with a unique shape and configuration. The attachment ensures efficient mixing by creating enhanced turbulence and shear within the mixture, leading to uniform results with reduced energy consumption. Its user-friendly design and compatibility with standard kitchen mixers make it a versatile and practical solution for both domestic and commercial kitchens.

The attachment is compatible with standard kitchen mixers and is made from food-grade, durable materials. Its easy-to-install and clean design ensures convenience for users. Description:[0001]  The present invention pertains to the technical field of industrial robotics, and more particularly relates to a subterranean drilling robot specifically adapted to locate gas leaks in buried pipelines. The invention integrates advanced drilling modules, omnidirectional sensing components, power and communication means, and a novel artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-based control system that enables autonomous decision-making and navigation toward suspected leakage points.
[0002]  The disclosed technology addresses the complexities of subterranean navigation, gas concentration gradient-based targeting, real-time image recognition, and adaptive steering. It provides a robust solution for improving the accuracy, speed, and safety of locating gas leakage positions in underground pipeline networks.

BACKGROUND 

[0003]  Buried pipelines are widely used worldwide to transport essential resources such as natural gas, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), hydrogen, and carbon dioxide. These hidden infrastructures are critical for industrial operations and daily energy supply. However, when leaks occur, the difficulty of accessing and visually inspecting these subterranean systems complicates timely and accurate leak detection.
[0004]  Current methods commonly rely on surface-based detectors and approximate leak positioning. Technicians often must excavate multiple times based on uncertain data, resulting in wasted time, labor, and materials. Moreover, for flammable and explosive substances like natural gas, rapid and precise localization of leaks is paramount to prevent catastrophic fire and explosion incidents.
[0005]  Conventional solutions fail to provide direct, underground-level sensing and navigation. The gas leaking from a pipeline is often diluted or altered before reaching above-ground detectors, leading to inaccuracies in pinpointing the leak source. Surface disturbances, ground wind, and soil density variations exacerbate the problem. Hence, an underground-capable robot that can navigate through soil, detect gas concentrations, and perform image-based recognition of pipeline structures would significantly enhance leak localization efforts.
[0006]  The prior art has not adequately addressed integrating a fully subterranean drilling robot with advanced AI-based controls for adaptive movement. Traditional robots may lack intelligent real-time decision-making and machine learning capabilities that can refine their approach, reduce downtime, and improve accuracy. Therefore, there exists a pressing need for a solution that leverages AI and ML to guide a drilling robot toward higher gas concentration gradients and potential leak sites, ensuring minimal guesswork and excavation.
[0007]  By combining mechanical drilling capabilities, omnidirectional gas sensing, imaging systems, position tracking, and AI/ML-driven navigation, the disclosed invention achieves a high degree of accuracy, efficiency, and safety in identifying buried pipeline leak points.

SUMMARY 
[0008]  The invention discloses an underground drilling robot equipped with a drilling module, an omnidirectional acquisition module, a power module, an intelligent control module, and a novel AI & ML-based control system. This integrated approach allows the robot to autonomously drill into soil, navigate complex underground routes, detect and analyze gas concentration gradients, capture front-end images, and correlate sensor data to identify leakage positions.
[0009]  The drilling module includes a conical head drill bit and multi-directionally adjustable rotating blades that grant the robot forward propulsion and steering capability in dense soil. By adjusting blade extension and retraction, the robot achieves fine-grained directional control.
[0010]  The omnidirectional acquisition module comprises multiple gas sensors distributed along the robot’s body to measure gas concentration from all directions, and an image collector at the front end to capture real-time subterranean visuals. These data streams feed into the intelligent control module and the AI/ML system, guiding the robot’s trajectory toward areas of higher gas concentration.
[0011]  The power module supplies energy to motors, sensors, and communication lines. It includes both external and built-in power supplies, as well as necessary wiring and motors for actuating the drilling and steering mechanisms.
[0012]  The intelligent control module comprises a control device, GPS positioning unit, signal receiver/transmitter, and a unique AI/ML subsystem. The AI/ML subsystem continuously learns from historical and real-time sensor data, refining the robot’s navigation strategy, predicting optimal drilling routes, and dynamically adjusting operational parameters. Such an adaptive control framework ensures that the robot converges on the leak location more rapidly and with fewer unnecessary detours.
[0013]  The invention offers significant improvements in accuracy, reduces the need for extensive trial-and-error excavations, and enhances operator safety. Its AI-driven predictive guidance allows swift localization of leaks, minimizing potential damage and enabling quicker emergency response.
Brief Description of the Drawings
[0014]  FIG. 1 is a The flowchart meticulously delineates the operational sequence of an AI/ML-driven subterranean drilling robot designed for precision localization of gas leakages within buried pipeline infrastructures..
[0015]  The process commences with the deployment of the robotic system above a suspected leakage zone, establishing the foundation for its autonomous excavation and navigation capabilities. Upon activation, the robot's head drill bit, equipped with conical and spiral configurations, initiates penetration into the soil, aided by rotational motion that ensures efficient advancement through varying densities of subterranean matter.
[0016]  As the drilling module progresses, the omnidirectional acquisition module simultaneously engages its suite of gas sensors and imaging apparatus to capture real-time environmental parameters, including multi-directional gas concentration gradients and forward-facing visuals. 
[0017]  These data streams are seamlessly relayed to the AI/ML-integrated control module, which serves as the decision-making epicenter of the system. Within this module, advanced machine learning algorithms perform intricate analyses of the incoming gas concentration differentials and image patterns, correlating these inputs to infer the most probable trajectory toward the gas leakage epicenter.
[0018]  At this juncture, the AI-driven logic bifurcates into two pathways: if the analysis identifies a positive concentration gradient, indicative of increasing gas proximity, the robot persists in its forward drilling trajectory. Conversely, should the sensor data fail to detect a favorable gradient, the multi-directionally adjustable rotating blades—controlled via telescopic actuators—undergo dynamic retraction and extension to execute a calculated steering maneuver, redirecting the robot toward a more promising vector of investigation.
[0019]  As the robot advances further into the subterranean terrain, the AI/ML system continuously scrutinizes the front-end imagery to detect recognizable pipeline structural features. Should the image collector identify anomalies consistent with pipeline surfaces, such as weld seams or corrosion points, the system transitions into a verification phase wherein it corroborates these findings with stabilized gas concentration levels. 
[0020]  A sustained high plateau in gas readings, coupled with visual confirmation of the pipeline, serves as a conclusive indicator of the leakage position.
[0021]  Upon pinpointing the leak source, the robot invokes its localization mechanism—utilizing GPS data or an auxiliary underground positioning system—to log precise coordinates of the identified site. [0023]  In its entirety, the process culminates in the seamless orchestration of mechanical drilling prowess, sensor fusion, and adaptive AI-based control. By continuously interpreting real-time sensor inputs and refining its navigational strategy through machine learning, the robot eliminates unnecessary excavation, expedites the detection process, and minimizes operator intervention.
[0024]  The result is a highly intelligent, self-optimizing system that achieves unparalleled accuracy, efficiency, and safety in the critical task of locating gas leakages within complex underground pipeline networks.
