Example 3: Process for Preparation of the Treatment System
The preparation process for the treatment system involves the formulation of nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), scaffold fabrication, incorporation of NLCs into scaffolds, and preparation of oral probiotics.

Step 1: Preparation of Nanostructured Lipid Carriers (NLCs)
The synthetic drug (Mesalamine) and the herbal drug (Epigallocatechin Gallate Hydrate) are dissolved in a blend of solid lipids (Glyceryl Monostearate and Palmitic Acid) and liquid lipids (Labrasol and Castor Oil). The lipid phase is heated to 80°C to ensure complete dissolution. Separately, an aqueous phase containing surfactants (Tween 80 and TPGS) is prepared under constant stirring. The lipid phase is then emulsified into the aqueous phase using high-speed homogenization at 2000 rpm, followed by sonication to reduce particle size to the nano range (approximately 121.9 nm). The resultant emulsion is stabilized and cooled to room temperature.

Step 2: Fabrication of Multifunctional Scaffolds
Collagen Type I and Chitosan are dissolved in an aqueous solution containing polyethylene glycol (PEG 4000) as a porosity agent and sodium chloride as a stabilizer. The solution is crosslinked using glutaraldehyde to enhance stability and is then lyophilized to produce porous scaffolds. The porous structure facilitates moisture retention and effective drug loading.

Step 3: Incorporation of NLCs into Scaffolds
The prepared scaffolds are cut into circular discs of 8 mm diameter and immersed in the drug-loaded NLC suspension. The scaffolds are stirred gently at 500 rpm for 24 hours to allow absorption of the NLCs. After soaking, the NLC-loaded scaffolds are frozen at -70°C and subjected to lyophilization, ensuring the integrity of the NLCs and creating a drug-loaded scaffold matrix with sustained release properties.

Step 4: Preparation of Oral Probiotics
Probiotic strains, including Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium bifidum, and Saccharomyces boulardii, are cultured, harvested, and freeze-dried. The probiotics are then encapsulated into hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) capsules. Each capsule contains a standardized dose of 5 × 10^8 CFU of each strain, with excipients like starch used for stabilization.

Final Packaging
The drug-loaded scaffolds are packaged in sterile, airtight containers to ensure stability and sterility. The oral probiotics are stored in dry, sealed capsule containers to maintain viability. This comprehensive preparation process ensures the delivery of an innovative and effective treatment for diabetic foot ulcers, combining local wound care with systemic health support.

The present disclosure introduces a bio-responsive wound dressing with integrated microchip sensing 100 for advanced wound care, enabling real-time monitoring of healing progress and complications. The invention features a cellulose-based hydrogel matrix 102 to provide a biocompatible and moisture-retentive dressing environment. Miniaturized microchips 104 are embedded within the hydrogel to process data from biosensors, including a ph sensor 106 for detecting acidity or alkalinity changes and a temperature sensor 108 for monitoring wound temperature. A wireless communication module 110 transmits real-time biomarker data to a mobile application 114 for remote monitoring and healthcare provider access. The system is powered by a biocompatible power source 112, ensuring uninterrupted functionality. An integrated alert system 116 notifies healthcare providers of critical wound conditions. Together, these components deliver a novel, efficient, and patient-friendly system for improving wound care outcomes and facilitating timely medical intervention. Reference Fig 1

Description:DETAILED DESCRIPTION   
[0015] The disclosed herbal ointment composition with antimicrobial potential utilizes a methanol extract of Jasminum humile as its key active ingredient. Jasminum humile, commonly known as Yellow Jasmine, is a plant recognized for its medicinal properties, particularly its antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing effects. The leaves of this plant contain bioactive compounds, including flavonoids, alkaloids, and tannins, which are known for their antibacterial and antioxidant activities. Leveraging these properties, the disclosed herbal ointment aims to provide a natural, effective alternative to synthetic topical antimicrobial agents.
[0016] The preparation process begins with the extraction of the active compounds from the leaves of Jasminum humile. A total of 500 g of dried leaf powder is subjected to methanol extraction using a Soxhlet extractor, which operates at a controlled temperature of 60°C for a duration of 7 hours. Methanol is chosen as the solvent for its ability to effectively extract polar and semi-polar bioactive compounds. The Soxhlet extraction method allows continuous washing of the leaf powder with methanol, ensuring maximum yield of the active compounds. After extraction, the methanol extract undergoes filtration through Whatman filter paper (No. 1), which removes particulate matter and impurities, resulting in a purified extract. The purified extract is then concentrated using a rotary evaporator under vacuum at 40°C to remove excess methanol while preserving the thermolabile bioactive compounds. To maintain its efficacy and stability, the concentrated extract is stored at a freezing temperature of -80°C until further use.
[0017] The ointment base is prepared using the fusion method, which involves heating the base components to a melting temperature of 70°C. The components, which may include natural oils, waxes, and emulsifiers, are melted and homogenized under controlled conditions to form a smooth, uniform base. Continuous stirring is performed during cooling to prevent phase separation and ensure consistency. The methanol extract of Jasminum humile is incorporated into the ointment base through trituration using a mortar and pestle. This process facilitates the even distribution of the active compounds within the ointment base, ensuring a uniform product that maximizes the therapeutic potential of the extract. The completed herbal ointment is then packaged into collapsible tubes for easy application and stored at room temperature.
[0018] The herbal ointment composition is evaluated through a comprehensive set of tests to assess its physicochemical properties and antimicrobial efficacy. The physical characteristics of the ointment, including its light green color, characteristic odor, and smooth consistency, are confirmed through visual examination. The pH of the formulation is measured at 7.2 using a digital pH meter, which is optimal for skin compatibility and ensures that the ointment does not cause irritation. The spreadability of the ointment, a crucial parameter for ease of application, is evaluated by placing the ointment between two slides and measuring the time required to separate them under a set weight. The result of 4 seconds indicates excellent spreadability. Extrudability is another critical factor, measured as the weight of the ointment required to extrude a 0.5 cm ribbon in 10 seconds, with a result of 0.6 g indicating good ease of use. Additional tests include loss on drying (LOD), which measures moisture content and yields a value of 20%, and washability, which demonstrates that the ointment is easy to remove with water.
[0019] The antimicrobial efficacy of the ointment is tested against Escherichia coli (E. coli) using an agar diffusion method. In this test, different concentrations of the ointment are applied to agar plates inoculated with E. coli, and the zones of inhibition are measured after 24 hours of incubation. For an ointment containing 25 mg/g of the methanol extract, a zone of inhibition measuring 1.7 cm is observed, while a concentration of 50 mg/g shows a larger zone of inhibition at 2.9 cm. These results confirm the potent antimicrobial activity of the ointment, making it a promising candidate for use as a natural antibacterial agent.
[0020] The stability of the ointment is tested under various storage conditions, including temperatures of 20°C, 25°C, and 35°C, and the formulation is found to remain stable without significant changes in its properties. The ointment’s non-irritant nature, combined with its good spreadability, extrudability, and washability, makes it user-friendly and suitable for regular topical application.
[0021] The herbal ointment composition presents a compelling case as a natural alternative to synthetic topical medications. Its reliance on the bioactive compounds of Jasminum humile offers a safer and potentially more sustainable approach to addressing bacterial skin infections. Future research may focus on further optimizing the formulation parameters, exploring its efficacy against a broader range of pathogens, and conducting clinical trials to establish its therapeutic potential in real-world settings. Additionally, efforts could be directed towards improving the scalability of the production process, ensuring that this innovative solution is accessible to a wider audience.

Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to the field of air purification, specifically to devices designed for the removal of fumes and airborne particles generated during soldering processes. This includes, but is not limited to, applications in electronics assembly, jewelry making, and other industrial or hobbyist settings where soldering is performed. The invention also touches on the subfields of mechanical ventilation and filtration technologies.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Soldering is an important process in many industries, including electronics, plumbing, and metalworking. However, it emits toxic fumes and airborne particles that pose serious health risks. These byproducts primarily consist of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), fine particulate matter, and metal oxides produced during the heating of solder and flux. Prolonged exposure to these contaminants can cause respiratory irritation, allergic reactions, and more serious long-term health problems like chronic respiratory disease or neurological issues. Despite the widespread use of soldering in various industries, addressing the health risks associated with its byproducts remains a major challenge.
Traditional fume extraction systems are widely used to reduce these risks in industrial settings. These systems frequently consist of large, stationary units outfitted with powerful extraction fans and multi-stage filtration systems. Such setups can effectively capture and filter a wide range of airborne pollutants. However, their large size, high cost, and reliance on fixed installations make them unsuitable for smaller workshops, educational environments, or home-based settings. Because of these limitations, a large portion of the soldering community is exposed to potentially harmful fumes and lacks access to adequate protective measures.
In response to these challenges, portable fume extractors have emerged as a viable alternative to fixed systems. These devices are designed to be compact, lightweight, and mobile, making them ideal for people who work in small spaces. While portable solutions improve accessibility and flexibility, they frequently fall short in terms of performance. Many lack adequate airflow capacity, effective filtration mechanisms, or the ability to capture finer particles and a diverse range of contaminants. This reduces their effectiveness, especially in environments involving heavy or prolonged soldering activities.
Another limitation of existing portable solutions is their inefficiency in dealing with the diverse byproducts of soldering. For example, some models may only address larger particles while failing to filter out VOCs and ultrafine particles, which can travel deep into the respiratory system. This inconsistency in performance reduces their usefulness as comprehensive air quality management tools. Furthermore, some portable extractors use low-cost, single-stage filters that saturate quickly and require frequent replacement, resulting in higher maintenance costs over time.
The absence of effective, affordable, and portable fume extraction devices leaves a significant gap in the market, particularly for hobbyists, small businesses, and educational facilities. Individuals in these situations are frequently forced to improvise with suboptimal solutions, such as using fans to redirect fumes or relying on makeshift filters that provide insufficient protection. Such approaches fail to address the underlying cause of the problem and may even introduce new risks by dispersing contaminants into surrounding areas.
Furthermore, as people become more aware of the health risks associated with poor indoor air quality, there is a greater demand for better fume extraction solutions. With a growing regulatory focus on workplace safety and personal health, businesses and individuals are looking for devices that meet stricter safety standards. However, the gap between these requirements and the capabilities of current portable systems remains, highlighting the urgent need for innovation in this area.
Filtration and airflow management technology advancements provide potential solutions to these challenges. Portable fume extractors could benefit from innovations like activated carbon filters, HEPA-grade filtration, and more efficient fan designs. However, incorporating these technologies into a compact, cost-effective design that is still accessible to a large user base necessitates careful engineering and design considerations.
Another promising avenue is the creation of smart fume extraction systems with sensors and automation. For example, devices equipped with air quality sensors could track pollutant levels in real time and adjust their performance accordingly. Such features not only increase efficiency, but they also provide users with greater convenience and confidence in the device's performance.
While existing solutions for soldering fume extraction address some of the health and safety concerns, significant gaps remain, especially for non-industrial users. There is a critical need for a small, efficient, and inexpensive device that can effectively remove soldering fumes and airborne particles. Such a solution would protect users' health, improve indoor air quality, and meet the growing demand for readily available safety measures in a variety of soldering environments.

Description:REAL-TIME BIDIRECTIONAL INDIAN SIGN LANGUAGE TRANSLATION AND LEARNING SYSTEM
FIELD OF THE INVENTION
This invention relates to the field of assistive communication technology, specifically focusing on real-time translation between sign language and spoken/written language. It also encompasses aspects of artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and human-computer interaction. The invention has applications in the subfields of natural language processing, gesture recognition, and interactive learning platforms.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Assistive communication technologies for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community play an important role in promoting inclusivity, but their current offerings are limited in scope and functionality. Many existing tools focus on translating sign language into text or speech, or vice versa, but they frequently lack bidirectional capabilities that enable seamless communication between signers and non-signers. This limitation significantly reduces their usefulness in dynamic, real-world scenarios where two-way communication is required.
Real-time translation presents a significant challenge for many of these technologies. Tools that attempt to translate sign language gestures into text or speech frequently experience latency, making natural conversation difficult. Furthermore, the lack of real-time translation capabilities from text or speech back into sign language creates a gap in mutual understanding because non-signers are unable to effectively convey their responses in a format that deaf and hard-of-hearing people can understand.Another critical limitation of existing tools is that they rely on static gesture databases. These databases frequently lack the ability to adapt to regional or user-specific differences in signing styles, which are common in languages such as Indian Sign Language (ISL). As a result, tools claiming to be universal may fail to capture the nuances of various linguistic and cultural contexts, resulting in inaccuracies and a poor user experience.
Mobile apps and virtual classrooms are examples of interactive learning platforms for sign language, which allow for self-paced education. However, they frequently fall short of providing personalized feedback and dynamic visual aids that are tailored to individual learning requirements. Many tools provide static lessons that ignore the user's progress, mistakes, or unique signing style. This lack of personalization reduces their effectiveness in developing language skills.
Some existing solutions, such as "SignAll," focus on sign-to-text or sign-to-speech translation for ISL gestures but do not provide text-to-sign functionality, rendering communication incomplete. Others, such as the "DEF-ISL App," are primarily intended for ISL learning, with an emphasis on vocabulary and grammar but no real-time translation or practical application in conversational contexts.
The lack of multilingual support is another barrier to inclusivity. In a linguistically diverse country like India, where ISL coexists with many spoken languages, the lack of tools capable of supporting regional languages adds another layer of complexity. Deaf and hard-of-hearing people frequently face communication difficulties, not only due to their hearing impairment, but also due to the limited linguistic flexibility of the tools at their disposal.
Context-awareness is an important but often overlooked feature in assistive communication tools. To ensure accurate interpretation, sign language relies heavily on context. Tools that lack the ability to include situational or conversational context in their translations frequently produce ambiguous or irrelevant results. This deficiency severely limits the effectiveness of such technologies in facilitating meaningful communication.
The acute shortage of certified ISL interpreters emphasizes the need for strong assistive technologies. Interpreters are frequently unavailable in critical situations like medical emergencies or legal proceedings, resulting in significant delays and miscommunications. A comprehensive technological solution could help bridge this gap by allowing deaf and hard-of-hearing people to navigate such situations independently.
The current state of assistive communication technology for the deaf and hard-of-hearing population is fragmented and insufficient. Tools that lack bidirectional communication, real-time capabilities, regional language support, and adaptive learning features fail to meet the community's diverse needs. These gaps highlight the critical need for an inclusive, adaptable, and user-friendly solution that empowers individuals and allows for seamless communication across diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

The principal object of the present invention is to develop a a comprehensive application for real-time, bidirectional translation between Indian Sign Language (ISL) and text/speech.
Another object of the present invention is to a comprehensive application for real-time, bidirectional translation between Indian Sign Language (ISL) and text/speech which ensures effective communication in professional, personal, and emergency situations.
Another object of the present invention is to a comprehensive application for real-time, bidirectional translation between Indian Sign Language (ISL) and text/speech which is user-friendly, and accessible tool for closing communication gaps in the deaf and hard-of-hearing communities

Existing technologies fall short because they do not support real-time, bidirectional communication between signers and non-signers. These restrictions impede access to critical services, education, employment, and social interactions, exacerbating isolation and limiting opportunities for the deaf community. Furthermore, the absence of multilingual support and adaptive learning features limits their applicability in linguistically diverse areas. The acute shortage of certified Indian Sign Language (ISL) interpreters exacerbates these challenges, particularly in emergency or critical situations requiring immediate communication.

Description:FIELD OF INVENTION

[001] The present invention relates to a field of automotive audio. Particularly, the present invention relates to a subwoofer enclosure in an automotive. More particularly, the present invention relates to the subwoofer enclosure designed for being mounted inside a center console of the automotive consisting of two parts with multiple integrated features, thereby utilizing maximum space and providing a cost saving subwoofer enclosure. 

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[002] Subwoofers provide low frequency bass sound. Subwoofer assembly in an automotive consists of one or more speakers mounted onto a rigid enclosure, usually having a large enclosed volume for providing improved audio quality. The enclosure should be sealed airtight. The volume of enclosed air required for good audio performance is calculated by audio experts. It varies with the type of subwoofer speaker used. Commonly, it is in the range of around 20 liters. Due to such large volume requirement, different positions have been proposed inside the automotive like under the seat, in the trunk area, near spare tire, inside center console etc. 

[003] Mounting strategies like hooks, snap fits, clips etc. lead to complicated manufacturing molds. The mounting strategy needs to be enabled for easy and repeatable mounting and unmounting. The enclosure shape again needs to be ensured for utilization of maximum space available inside front center console, since large enclosed volumes improve sound quality.

[004] The enclosure requires to be rigid and strong enough to take load of the speaker vibrations, and sustain jerks and vibrations of moving vehicle. The constituting parts of enclosure are needed to be manufactured by injection molding and avoid any undercuts in the manufacturing mold (slider, cores etc.) for cost reduction. 

[005] Generally, separate molds are required for manufacturing coupling parts, due to differences in the coupling features. For interlocking two parts, separate molds are needed to make a male part and a female part. 

[006] A patent document US20240137691A1 titled “Front center vehicle console with speakers” discloses a cubic enclosure for subwoofer speakers, with stiffening columns between them. The enclosure may be one piece, or made of 2 constituting pieces or 3 constituting pieces. It also mentions about an enclosure that can be assembled from two half-enclosure pieces and fixed together with sufficient airtightness. Enclosure shape can be cylindrical or cubic or prismatic.

[007] Another patent document US5532437A titled “Speaker assembly” discloses a speaker assembly for a motor vehicle in which the speaker is mounted to a blow molded enclosure so as to minimize vibration of the enclosure. The speaker includes a back plate and a frame with a peripheral flange. The enclosure has front and rear wall portions, the front wall portion defining an opening for receiving the speaker. Adjacent the opening, the front wall portion has a planar sealing surface for supporting the flange. A gasket is provided intermediate the flange and the sealing surface. A fastener extends through the rear wall portion and engages the back plate of the speaker. The fastener draws the flange towards the sealing surface and compresses the gasket. The speaker spaces the rear wall portion a fixed distance from the front wall portion. A flat speaker wire conveniently extends into the enclosure through the same opening that receives the speaker.

[008] Yet another patent document EP2119598B1 titled “Speaker assembly arrangement and method of mounting a speaker” discloses a method of mounting a subwoofer box on vehicle. It couples the subwoofer box to another enclosure formed by vehicles body in order to increase the resonant volume. The design of the enclosure is divided into first volume and second volume. The connection is acoustically sealed and waterproof. Press fit coupling is used, a sealing ring ensures airtight joining of the two volumes. Fastening on vehicle body is done using screw or snap fit fastening. Snap fit leads to undercuts, and gets damaged after few cycles of mounting and unmounting.

[009] Another patent document CN214014453U titled “Box front cover of sound box and combined sound box” discloses a design of a sound box body consisting of front cover plate and back body. This sound box can hold midrange speakers as well as bass speakers. This is an injection molded part with integrated features like separation plate, cavities for two different types of speakers, separation of the sound box into upper and lower zone, etc. The front cover and rear cover are two separate parts which will need separate manufacturing molds. This invention is not specifically for automobile application.

[0010] One another patent document CN203047053U titled “Installing structure of subwoofer and vehicle” discloses a subwoofer casing and its mounting method to utilize maximum available space inside boot of a car, adjacent to spare tire. It suggests the enclosure to be manufactured by blow moulding. Single speaker can be mounted only on top face of the enclosure. Speakers arranged facing away from each other result in cancellation of vibrations and give improved sound quality.

[0011] The prior art documents have a disadvantage that they do not mention about how the constituting parts are interlocked in position and any feature that help to mount the enclosure on vehicle. The clips and retainers are used in the prior art for mounting speaker, the manufacturing mold is complicated due to undercuts and cost increases. The prior art gives some demerits associated with injection molding:  high tooling and material cost, difficulty to achieve sealing of two combining parts and suggests a blow molded speaker enclosure. 

[0012] In order to overcome the problem associated with the state of arts, there is a need for the development of an enclosure for assembling a subwoofer that is easy to install, requires less components for fixing the enclosure and be installed in such a way that there is a more efficient air-tight enclosure with less expenditure.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0042] The present invention relates to an automotive subwoofer enclosure. The subwoofer enclosure of the automotive comprises of a mounting bracket coupled to a chassis of an automotive, a pair of covers joined to form the subwoofer enclosure which is affixed on the mounting bracket, and a pad placed between the covers forming an airtight sealing of the subwoofer enclosure. Further, the covers comprise a plurality of sets of bosses provided on the back of the covers, a first cut-out portion for providing outlet of a wire, and a second cut-out portion for providing mounting base for a pair of speakers connected on both ends of the covers.

[0043] The cover parts of the subwoofer enclosure have a unique edge design which interlocks the two cover parts in position during assembly, forms airtight sealed enclosure due to compression of a pad between a contoured edge on one cover part and flat edge on the other, enables same mold to produce both cover parts, without needing a mirror mold and all features are integrated without any undercuts in manufacturing mold.The present invention also provides a method for assembling of subwoofer enclosure. The method comprises steps of: attaching a pair of speakers on a pair of covers using screws, routing a wire of the speakers through a first-cutout, flipping one of the covers about the central horizontal axis to make the cover on right side of the enclosure, aligning left and right cover to face each other, positioning a pad at an outer edge of the left cover, interlocking the covers in position during which the first cutouts of the two joining covers align together to form a circle, inserting bolts through a first set of bosses from both sides and tightening, resulting in compression of the pad and forming an airtight seal between the covers, sealing the first cutout using a sealant and drilling a small decompression hole on one of the covers to balance the air pressure inside and outside the subwoofer enclosure in extreme operating conditions.

[0061] B) Pair of covers (108): The subwoofer enclosure (100) consists of two cover parts (108). The covers (108), as illustrated in combination of Figures 3-7, are joined together through bolts to form the subwoofer enclosure (100) which is affixed on the mounting bracket (102). Further, the covers (108) comprises a plurality of sets of bosses (110, 112, 114, 116) provided on the back of the covers (108), a unique dual functionality edge design for interlocking and efficient rubber compression, a first cut-out portion (118) for providing outlet of a speaker wire (120), and a second cut-out portion (122) for providing mounting base for a speaker (124) one speaker is mounted on each cover.

[0062] In an exemplary embodiment of the present invention, the covers (108) are tightened against the first and the second set of mating bosses (110, 112) through a plurality of bolts. All the bosses (110, 112, 114, 116) are integral part of the covers (108), manufactured during injection molding. Ribs are provided around the bosses (110, 112, 114, 116) for strength and rigidity. When the cover parts (108) are joined, the first and the second set of mating bosses (110, 112) act as a stepped column with different circular cross section. These columns add rigidity to the subwoofer enclosure (100), when compared to a hollow box without any columns.

[0063] In an embodiment, a first set of bosses (110) are provided for inserting bolts for joining the covers (108), a second set of bosses (112) are provided for tightening the bolts, a third set of bosses (114) are provided for the speaker (124) mounting screws and a fourth set of bosses (116) for the mounting bracket (102) bolts. The first and the second set of mating bosses (110, 112) of the two covers (108) serve dual functions by fastening the covers (108) through bolts and by acting as column stiffeners for the enclosure, as shown in figure 9b. 

[0064] In an exemplary embodiment, the first set of bosses (110) for inserting the bolt are plain cylindrical shaped, with diameter that accommodates bolt head. The first set of bosses (110) have holes to allow bolts to pass through them into their second set of mating bosses (112). The second set of mating bosses’ (112) diameter is chosen to ensure a tight fitment of threaded insert.

[0065] The same cover part (108) is flipped about central horizontal axis (400) to form its mating part (Figure 5b and 6). Positioning of the un-identical first and the second set of mating bosses (110, 112) is done strategically to ensure their mating during assembly with the flipped cover part (Figure 6 shows mating bosses in flipped cover part). 

[0066] In another embodiment, a horizontal central axis (400) divides the left cover (108) into upper and lower halves, as shown in Figure 5b. The upper half of the cover (108) has a flat edge (134) surface running along the outer joining walls. The pad (126) rests on this outer flat edge (134) in the upper half of the covers (108). An extended interlocking flange (500) is located adjacent to the flat edge (134), running along the inner walls. In lower half, the flat outer edge (134) of upper half changes into a contoured edge (132) surface. The pad (126) rests on the contoured edge (132) in lower half. The extended inner flange (500) of upper half changes into a stepped depression (600) in lower half. This inner stepped depression (600) is adjacent to the outer contoured edge (132).

[0067] Each cover part contains the first sets of bosses (110) and the second sets of bosses (112), for inserting and tightening bolt respectively. The bolts are inserted into first set of bosses (110) from both sides of the enclosure (100) and tightened. This joining method enables the enclosure (100) to be assembled and disassembled easily.

[0068] In another exemplary embodiment, the subwoofer enclosure (100) may be placed inside a center console (128) of the automotive (106). The center console (128) comprises of a third cut-out portion (130) for speaker’s sound propagation inside the cabin. The third cutout portion (130) is covered with a speaker grille for protection of speakers and improved aesthetics. 

[0069] In yet another exemplary embodiment, the left and right covers (108) are manufactured by plastic injection molding. The molding process allows use of variable wall thickness, addition of ribs, adding details like a contoured edge and achieves high dimensional accuracy. There are no undercuts in the cover part’s (108) design. Direction of bosses (110, 112, 114, 116) is along the tooling direction to avoid complicated manufacturing molds requiring sliders, cores etc. Threads are not added to bosses during injection molding. Instead, metallic threaded inserts are installed in the second, third and fourth set of bosses (112, 114, 116) after the process of injection molding. This further simplifies and reduces cost of the manufacturing mold. Pull tests on these inserts help to ensure that they are securely integrated with the cover part. Both Left and Right covers (108) is manufactured from the same mold. This helps to avoid cost of additional mold. Right cover (108) is formed by flipping the left cover (108) which saves cost for a mirror mold.
 
[0070] C) Pair of speakers (124): A pair of speakers (124) are connected on both ends of the enclosure (100). One speaker (124) is mounted on each cover (108).  The cover part has a circular supporting base with a central second cutout portion (122) and screw bosses (114) in its periphery for mounting the speakers (124) inside the subwoofer enclosure (100). Wall thickness of a supporting base is slightly higher than rest of the enclosure walls so that the enclosure (100) withstands higher load of the speakers’ (124) vibrations. The center console (128) comprises a third cut-out portion (130) corresponding to speakers (124) to allow sound propagation inside cabin.

[0071]  In an exemplary embodiment, during assembly, the speaker (124) is secured to the supporting base using screws. When mounting the speaker (124), a thin rubber pad is placed between the speaker’s (124) frame and the mounting base on covers (108) to ensure air-tight clamping of speaker (124) onto the cover (108). The covers (108) have a small first cutout portion (118) in the front which allows the wires (114) from speaker (124) to be routed outside the enclosure (100).

[0072]  In another exemplary embodiment, a rubber grommet is used to seal the first cutout portion (118) for the speaker wire (120).

[0073] D) Pad (126): A pad (126) is placed between the covers (108) forming an airtight sealing of the subwoofer enclosure (100) as shown in combination of Figures 8a-11. The pad (126) is adequately compressed (at least 20%) between the joining edges to ensures efficient sealing.  A rubber pad compressed by a contoured edge with convex protrusion is more effective than compression by a flat edge as shown in Figure 11.

[0074] In an embodiment, the pad (126) has a rectangular cross section and runs along the outer walls of joining edges of the enclosure (100). In an exemplary embodiment, the thickness of the pad (126) is 2mm and the pad (126) is selected form the material made of rubber, silicone and the like. 

[0075] In an exemplary embodiment, during assembly of the two cover parts (108), left cover and right cover are placed facing each other. Figure 7 shows the subwoofer enclosure (100) simplified by removing the bosses (110, 112, 114, 116), to focus on joining edges, the pad (126) is placed on the left cover’s outer edges. Right cover is moved closer till the extended flanges (500) on both covers (108) engage into their respective stepped depressions (600) creating an interlock. At this stage, the two covers (108) are held against each other in lateral direction, manually or using supports. The interlock arrests the movement of the covers (108) in vertical and longitudinal directions. After interlocking, the covers (108) are joined together by bolts which results in compression of the pad (126) between the covers (108) and creates an airtight sealing between the covers (108). In an exemplary embodiment, two simultaneous functions occur along the outer and inner walls. Along the inner walls: left cover’s extended flange (500) in upper half fits into the stepped depression (600) of right cover’s upper half. At the same time, stepped depression (600) in left cover’s lower half receives the extended flange (500) of right cover’s lower half. Along the outer walls:  Left cover’s flat outer edge (134) in upper half compresses the pad (126) against contoured edge (132) of right cover. In lower half, left cover’s outer contoured edge (132) compresses rubber pad (126) against the flat edge (134) of right cover (108).

[0002] Real-time Indian language translation to text using computer vision is an innovative approach aimed at enhancing accessibility and communication, particularly for individuals with hearing impairments or those facing language barriers. India, with its diverse linguistic landscape, making communication challenging for people who do not share a common language. The integration of computer vision and machine learning technologies offers a promising solution to bridge these linguistic gaps. Using deep learning algorithms and image processing techniques, computer vision systems can recognize handwritten or sign language gestures in real time and convert them into text or spoken language. This process typically involves using neural networks to identify visual patterns, such as hand movements, facial expressions, or handwritten characters, and translating them into a language that can be easily understood by the user.
[0003] By utilizing datasets of sign language, gestures, and other forms of visual communication in various Indian languages, these systems can improve accessibility in public spaces, educational institutions, and workplaces. The development of such technologies also helps preserve linguistic diversity while promoting inclusive communication. These advancements are crucial for enabling people with disabilities to participate more fully in society, as well as for facilitating multilingual communication in a country as diverse as India. The use of real-time translation via computer vision opens up new possibilities for automated, language-agnostic communication, reducing reliance on manual interpretation and fostering a more connected society. 
[0004] With continuous improvements in AI and computer vision techniques, such systems are expected to become more accurate and widely accessible, offering significant improvements in the lives of individuals from different linguistic backgrounds. This system is a real-time sign language recognition system designed to convert hand gestures into text and speech. The process begins with capturing images of hand gestures using a camera. Each class, representing a specific gesture, has a set of images collected and stored in directories. These images are processed to extract key features using MediaPipe, a library for detecting hand landmarks. These landmarks, which consist of x, y, and z coordinates for each point on the hand, are then normalized to create consistent data representations. The collected data is stored and later used for training a machine learning model.

Background

Food processing systems are widely employed for the preparation, handling, and packaging of food items to meet consumer demand. Among various food processing tasks, washing chips to remove debris, starch residues, and contaminants is a critical operation. Efficient washing processes are necessary to maintain the quality and safety of food products while ensuring compliance with health and safety regulations.
Conventional chip washing systems generally employ large mechanical assemblies that consume significant amounts of energy during operation. Furthermore, such systems frequently utilize high-capacity motors and pumps to facilitate the movement and cleaning of chips, which results in increased energy consumption. A major drawback of such systems is the inability to optimize energy usage, leading to excessive operational costs and environmental concerns associated with energy wastage.
Moreover, traditional chip washing systems often rely on fixed-speed motors and non-adaptive mechanisms to perform washing operations. Such mechanisms are typically incapable of adjusting energy consumption based on the load or operating conditions, thereby resulting in suboptimal energy utilization. Additionally, the fixed-speed operation contributes to higher wear and tear of mechanical components, increasing maintenance costs and downtime for such systems.
Another commonly employed chip washing technique involves the use of gravity-fed systems and large agitators. While such systems reduce reliance on active mechanical components, the lack of controlled motion and precision often leads to inconsistent washing results. Furthermore, such systems are frequently associated with water wastage due to non-recirculated water flow, further contributing to inefficiency.
Additionally, several existing chip washing systems incorporate belt conveyors to transport chips during washing operations. Such conveyors are generally powered by high-speed motors, which operate without any form of energy optimization. The absence of energy management mechanisms often leads to overheating and inefficiency in power usage. The maintenance of such high-speed motors and conveyor assemblies also contributes to increased operational expenses.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for washing chips, particularly to address issues of energy consumption, operational efficiency, and maintenance challenges.

The conveyance assembly includes a conveyor belt driven by a low-power motor, and an energy control unit is linked to the conveyance assembly to optimise power usage during operation.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Adhesive application techniques have long been utilised in industries such as manufacturing, packaging, and construction to enable the secure attachment of materials. Traditional systems for adhesive application generally rely on manual methods or semi-automated machinery. Manual methods require substantial operator effort and are often associated with inconsistent application of adhesive, leading to variability in bonding strength and reduced reliability in the resulting attachment. Such variability becomes particularly problematic in applications requiring high precision and durability.
Moreover, semi-automated adhesive application systems are commonly employed to address issues associated with manual methods. Such systems typically involve mechanisms to dispense adhesive in a controlled manner, often employing spray nozzles or rollers. However, the uniformity of adhesive application is frequently compromised due to improper alignment of applicators or irregularities in the target material. Furthermore, these systems often lack mechanisms to firmly secure materials during adhesive application, resulting in displacement or misalignment during processing.
Additional systems that employ automated roller-based adhesive application mechanisms are also known. Such mechanisms are often combined with auxiliary components to enhance adhesion. However, these systems commonly face limitations in achieving uniform pressure distribution across the material, particularly when applying adhesive to surfaces with grooves or patterns. Such limitations result in incomplete bonding and material separation under stress, reducing the reliability of adhesive fixation.
In further developments, curing arrangements have been introduced to expedite adhesive bonding. These arrangements typically involve heat or ultraviolet light-based curing techniques to solidify the adhesive. While effective, such arrangements are often bulky and energy-intensive, making them impractical for use in space-constrained environments or applications requiring low power consumption. Moreover, such curing techniques are frequently inadequate in providing uniform curing across the adhesive layer, leading to weak or brittle bonds in certain regions.
Another area of concern involves control systems integrated within adhesive application systems. Conventional control systems primarily manage dispensing rates and temperatures but lack real-time adaptability to material variations or adhesive viscosity changes. Such limitations often result in inefficiencies in adhesive usage and inconsistencies in bonding quality, particularly in high-volume production settings.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for adhesive application and fixation.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Concrete construction has traditionally relied on manual processes and semi-automated systems for assembly and placement. Conventional methods involve manual labour and standalone machines that often operate in isolation. Manual methods are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to human error, which may lead to inconsistencies in the quality of construction. Additionally, standalone machines require extensive operator intervention, limiting efficiency and consistency during construction operations.
Mechanised systems for concrete assembly and injection have been introduced to address these issues. Such systems often utilise independent lifting and injection devices to handle concrete placement and structural adjustments. However, such mechanised systems frequently lack synchronisation between lifting mechanisms and concrete application units. As a result, operational inefficiency arises, leading to uneven distribution, poor alignment, and delays during construction. Moreover, existing systems are unable to dynamically adjust based on feedback received from the construction process.
Furthermore, construction environments often involve uneven surfaces and varied structural configurations. Traditional assembly systems are ill-suited to adapt to such scenarios, resulting in limited versatility. Conventional systems also face challenges in accurately monitoring and adjusting lifting operations and mortar injection, particularly in dynamic or real-time conditions. The absence of integrated coordination mechanisms further compounds these limitations, reducing the overall reliability of construction activities.
Various attempts have been made to integrate feedback mechanisms into concrete assembly systems. However, such attempts are associated with challenges in achieving real-time synchronisation of multiple components. The absence of a unified approach to coordinate lifting and mortar injection further restricts the effectiveness of such systems. Inconsistent operation, maintenance requirements, and high costs further hinder the adoption of existing mechanised systems in large-scale or repetitive construction projects.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for concrete assembly and mortar injection during construction activities.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Robotic cleaning systems are widely adopted in residential and commercial environments to automate cleaning tasks. Such systems typically operate autonomously or semi-autonomously to eliminate the manual effort associated with traditional cleaning methods. Existing robotic cleaning systems utilise various locomotion mechanisms and cleaning technologies to perform cleaning operations.
One commonly known type of robotic cleaning system employs rotating brushes or rollers to agitate and dislodge debris from a surface. Such systems often lack effective mechanisms to adapt to varying surface types or conditions, leading to reduced cleaning performance. Further, the cleaning components of such systems frequently experience wear and tear, resulting in high maintenance requirements and limited operational longevity.
Another known category of robotic cleaning systems incorporates suction-based mechanisms to collect debris and particles from surfaces. However, conventional systems employing suction devices encounter limitations in managing large or heavy debris, often necessitating manual intervention. Additionally, such systems are unable to efficiently segregate collected debris, leading to inefficient waste disposal processes.
Moreover, robotic cleaning systems are generally equipped with rudimentary obstacle detection and navigation systems. Such systems primarily rely on basic sensors or predefined path algorithms, which restrict adaptability to dynamic environments. As a result, navigation inefficiencies often arise, causing incomplete cleaning coverage and frequent collisions with obstacles.
Further, several robotic cleaning systems are powered by battery sources, which often suffer from limited energy efficiency. Conventional power sources require frequent recharging, reducing operational uptime and overall cleaning effectiveness. Furthermore, such systems frequently lack mechanisms to optimise power usage, leading to unnecessary energy wastage.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for robotic cleaning operations, including limitations in cleaning performance, debris management, navigation efficiency, and energy utilisation.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Cleaning systems are generally employed to maintain cleanliness and hygiene in containers used in various industries such as food, beverage, pharmaceuticals, and chemicals. Such containers are frequently exposed to residues that accumulate over time, necessitating regular cleaning to avoid contamination and ensure operational efficiency. Furthermore, maintaining consistent cleanliness standards is critical for compliance with regulations associated with different industrial sectors.
Conventional cleaning techniques include manual cleaning, where human intervention is required to scrub and clean containers. Such a method is labour-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to human error. Moreover, manual cleaning often fails to achieve uniform cleaning results across different surfaces and crevices of the containers, leading to suboptimal hygiene standards. Furthermore, dependence on human labour for such repetitive tasks frequently results in increased costs and decreased operational efficiency.
Automated cleaning systems have been developed to address challenges associated with manual cleaning. Such systems typically rely on fixed cleaning mechanisms designed to clean containers of specific shapes and sizes. However, such automated systems lack flexibility and adaptability to accommodate containers of varying dimensions, shapes, and materials. Moreover, such systems are often prone to wear and tear due to repetitive movements and may require frequent maintenance, leading to downtime and increased operational expenses.
Furthermore, conventional automated systems often lack mechanisms to self-maintain and adapt to dynamic cleaning requirements. This limitation further results in the inefficiency of cleaning operations, particularly in industries that handle containers requiring frequent cleaning cycles. Additionally, issues such as the inability to remove persistent stains and residues from hard-to-reach areas of containers remain unaddressed in many conventional cleaning systems.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for cleaning containers.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Manufacturing processes commonly involve stamping techniques to imprint desired patterns or shapes onto objects. Traditional systems often employ mechanical stamping systems relying on manual alignment of objects. Such systems are prone to misalignments and errors during stamping, leading to defects in stamped objects. Further, reliance on manual intervention increases operational inefficiency and extends production timelines.
Moreover, conventional systems use adhesive application methods for securing components during production. Adhesive application in known systems is often inconsistent due to manual control or poorly integrated mechanisms. Inconsistent adhesive application results in weak bonds, compromising the structural integrity of manufactured objects. Additionally, the lack of synchronisation between stamping and adhesive application operations causes production delays and quality degradation.
Further, known methods for holding stamped objects within the production process often employ static or mechanical jigs that lack adaptability to varying shapes or sizes of objects. Such limitations restrict the flexibility of production lines, necessitating frequent reconfigurations, which result in downtime and reduced productivity.
Monitoring and quality control in traditional stamping and adhesive application processes are commonly performed through manual inspections or basic sensor systems. Such systems are unable to detect subtle errors or deviations in real-time, leading to defects escaping detection until later stages. Moreover, standalone monitoring systems lack integration with other production processes, limiting their effectiveness in ensuring consistent quality.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for stamping, adhesive application, and quality monitoring in manufacturing processes.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
Illumination devices have been extensively utilised in various applications, including industrial, residential, and commercial settings. Such devices commonly include light sources integrated with optical components to provide adequate lighting. Despite their widespread adoption, illumination devices are frequently associated with limitations that hinder efficiency and performance in demanding environments.
One well-known type of illumination device employs a light source integrated with a basic lens assembly. Such devices typically provide non-uniform light distribution, resulting in the formation of hotspots and uneven illumination. These issues are particularly evident in scenarios requiring focused lighting or high precision. Moreover, the fixed design of lens assemblies restricts the customisation of light projection, which is often required for specific applications.
Another commonly employed illumination system incorporates a combination of diffusers and reflectors to enhance light distribution. Such systems, while improving light dispersion to some extent, frequently introduce energy losses due to absorption and scattering. The bulky construction of such systems also adds to installation and maintenance challenges, limiting the overall practicality of said systems.
Furthermore, illumination devices relying on static configurations fail to adapt to variable lighting requirements. This lack of adaptability often necessitates additional components to achieve desired lighting characteristics, increasing costs and complexity. In addition, the inefficiency of conventional systems in minimising energy consumption and reducing glare remains a significant challenge.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and/or techniques for achieving uniform illumination and minimising hotspots in a compact and efficient manner.

Background
The background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art.
The present disclosure generally relates to devices and systems for mechanical assembly involving components requiring alignment and secure positioning during installation. Further, such systems are widely employed in various fields where precision and stability are critical to operational efficiency.
Conventional techniques for assembling components, particularly those requiring secure insertion into adjustment conduits, often rely on manual handling or rudimentary tools. Manual techniques are prone to alignment errors, leading to potential damage to the components or suboptimal functionality. Moreover, reliance on manual expertise can result in inconsistent outcomes across operations. Additionally, the use of basic tools often fails to provide the required accuracy, especially for applications necessitating stringent tolerances.
Furthermore, automated systems are also commonly employed in assembly operations. Such automated systems typically utilise robotic arms or similar mechanisms to manipulate components during assembly. However, the complexity of such systems often results in increased costs and extensive maintenance requirements. Moreover, the inability of such systems to adapt to varied component geometries without significant reconfiguration limits their versatility.
Another widely known technique involves employing mechanical jigs or fixtures to facilitate component alignment during assembly. Although such fixtures offer enhanced stability compared to manual methods, the fixed configurations of such jigs often restrict their adaptability to components of varying dimensions or shapes. Additionally, excessive reliance on fixed fixtures may lead to increased setup times, thus reducing overall operational efficiency.
Moreover, the use of pneumatic or hydraulic systems for applying force during assembly is also prevalent. Such systems are generally capable of achieving higher force magnitudes but are frequently associated with challenges, including leakage risks, the need for precise pressure regulation, and maintenance concerns. Furthermore, the bulkiness of such systems limits their application in compact setups.
In light of the above discussion, there exists an urgent need for solutions that overcome the problems associated with conventional systems and techniques for aligning and inserting components into adjustment conduits.
